Patients with advanced cancer and those near the end of life are commonly administered opioid via subcutaneous injection or continuous infusion. Compared with intravenous administration, this route requires less training to use, is less painful and can be used in the community. A continuous subcutaneous infusion over 24 hours of opioid using a syringe driver can provide highly effective background pain relief, mimicking pain control produced by taking modified-release opioid. Breakthrough pain is then managed using bolus subcutaneous opioid injections, which work faster than oral immediate-release opioid.
